content: Every finite verb so far has been
INDICATIVE: a verb stating a fact.
Latin has a second mood for verbs that
state none. It is the SUBJUNCTIVE, and
it marks a clause as something other
than plain report — a purpose, a result,
a reported question, a supposition.
This card's own sentence supposes what
never happened:
quae sī stetisset rēs pūblica
vōvissem
= vows I would have made, had the
republic still been standing
stetisset and vōvissem are subjunctive.
The republic did not stand; the vows
were never made. The mood says so.
The mood shows in a letter or two.
PRESENT — the vowel before the ending
shifts:
amat  → amet      videt → videat
regit → regat     audit → audiat
est → sit      potest → possit
vult → velit   scit → sciat
IMPERFECT — the infinitive with a
personal ending on it:
amāret   vidēret   regeret
audīret  esset     vellet
PERFECT — -eri-: docuerit, crēverit
PLUPERFECT — -isse-: stetisset, mōvisset
One mood, several jobs. The clause it
sits in decides which:
cum + subj.        when, since
ut, nē + subj.     in order that
ut + signal word   so that (result)
quid, cūr + subj.  a reported question
Lessons 36 to 38 name each of the three
commonest in turn.
A perfect subjunctive in -erit and a
future perfect indicative in -erit are
spelled alike. The clause tells them
apart: a cum-clause or a reported
question takes the mood.
Recognition only. Spot the mood, then
read what its clause is doing — nothing
here asks you to build one.
cum arrives three ways, and only what
stands beside it tells them apart.
PREPOSITION with an ablative, 'with':
cum Caesare — with Caesar
cum with an INDICATIVE — plain time:
cum vēnit — when he came
cum with a SUBJUNCTIVE — the clause
does more than mark a moment. This
card's own sentence:
cum ... tantus morbus oppresserit
= when so great a sickness has
struck him down
oppresserit is perfect subjunctive. No
second word marks the clause off — the
mood alone does it.
Two jobs share that one shape.
CIRCUMSTANTIAL — it sets the scene the
main verb happens in:
cum flūmen dēcrēsceret, imperātor
exercitum trānsīre iussit
= when the river was falling, the
commander ordered the army across
CAUSAL — it gives the reason:
cum eum magnitūdō victimae mōvisset
= since the size of the victim had
moved him
English must choose: when, after, since,
although. The story decides, as with the
ablative absolute (Lesson 30). In past
narrative, expect the subjunctive.
ut with a subjunctive most often marks
PURPOSE — why the thing was done.
Negative purpose takes nē, never ut nōn.
This card's own sentence:
Metellus cōnspectum Marī fūgerat, nē
vidēret ea quae ... nequīverat
= Metellus had fled the sight of
Marius, so as not to see what he
had been unable to bear
English shrinks such a clause to a bare
infinitive, 'to see'. Latin keeps a
clause with a finite verb in it.
quō stands in for ut before a
comparative:
quō sit studiōsior — so that he may
be the keener
The same ut with a subjunctive can mark
RESULT — what followed, not what was
meant. A signal word in the main clause
is the cue: tam, ita, sīc, adeō, tantus,
tālis, is.
Ita plērumque ēvenit, ut ... alium
quaerat
= that is generally how it turns out,
that he looks for another
Is splendor est vestrum ut eadem
postulentur
= such is your standing that the same
things are demanded
A negated result keeps ut nōn: ut tē
nōn tollerem, 'that I did not take you'.
That nē / ut nōn split is the one sure
test between the two.
A question can be reported instead of
asked. Latin keeps the question word and
puts its verb into the subjunctive.
This card's own sentence:
Dē Crabrā quid agātur ... velim
scīre
= I should like to know how matters
stand with the Crabra
agātur is present subjunctive. Nothing
else marks the clause, and the sentence
as a whole is not a question.
The question word comes first. The verb
of asking, knowing or seeing can stand
well away from it, even last.
Tense is read against that verb.
Any question word can open one:
quis, quid, quī    who, what, which
ubi, unde, quō     where
cūr, quārē         why
quantum, quālis    how much, what sort
num, an, -ne       whether
Vidēbis quid Curiō, quid medicō
placeat
= you will see what suits Curius,
what suits the doctor
Adfert quās ille post id tempus
fābulās docuerit
= he points out which plays that man
staged after that date
Lesson 34's habit, in question form:
find the reporting verb, read under it.
